clinicalPearls: Martorell ulcer is a painful ischaemic skin ulcer caused by subcutaneous arteriolosclerosis, arising almost exclusively in patients with long-standing, often poorly controlled arterial hypertension and frequently coexisting type 2 diabetes
It characteristically affects the dorsolateral aspect of the lower leg or the region overlying the Achilles tendon, and is bilateral in a substantial proportion of cases
The pain is severe and disproportionate to ulcer size; lesions begin as a livid or purpuric patch that rapidly breaks down into a necrotic ulcer with an irregular, often serpiginous, advancing border
Peripheral pulses are typically preserved and the ankle-brachial index is normal, which helps distinguish it from large-vessel atherosclerotic arterial ulceration

Diagnosis rests on the combination of hypertension or diabetes, the characteristic site and disproportionate pain, and a deep wedge biopsy from the ulcer edge showing arteriolosclerosis with medial calcification and subintimal proliferation
It is frequently mistaken for pyoderma gangrenosum, and inappropriate immunosuppression may worsen the wound and delay correct treatment

Management centres on optimising blood pressure control, meticulous wound care with debridement of necrotic tissue, and adequate analgesia, while avoiding strongly vasoconstricting agents where feasible
Early split-skin grafting, sometimes aided by negative-pressure wound therapy, can markedly reduce pain and accelerate healing
reference.pathophysiology: The primary lesion in Martorell ulcer lies in the subcutaneous small arteries and arterioles, which develop medial hypertrophy and calcification together with subintimal (myointimal) proliferation as a consequence of chronic arterial hypertension and diabetic microvascular disease. Progressive luminal narrowing of these vessels critically reduces dermal and subcutaneous perfusion, so that a comparatively minor rise in local tissue pressure or trivial trauma produces a cutaneous infarct. Because the occlusive process is confined to the microcirculation, the large conduit arteries remain patent and pulses are preserved, yet the ischaemic skin necroses and ulcerates, extending as the surrounding arterioles are progressively compromised.
additionalDifferentials: Vasculitic ulcer, such as in polyarteritis nodosa or other systemic vasculitis
additionalInvestigations: Deep incisional or wedge biopsy taken from the ulcer edge for histology demonstrating subcutaneous arteriolosclerosis
Ankle-brachial index and arterial duplex ultrasound to exclude significant large-vessel disease
Blood pressure assessment, including ambulatory monitoring, to gauge control
Glycaemic assessment with glucose and glycated haemoglobin
Screen for calciphylaxis with calcium, phosphate, parathyroid hormone and renal function
Autoimmune and vasculitis screen to exclude mimics
Wound tissue culture if secondary infection is suspected
redFlags: Rapidly enlarging necrotic ulcer with pain out of proportion to its appearance
Signs of secondary wound infection or systemic sepsis
Features suggesting calciphylaxis, such as renal failure or dialysis dependence with painful skin necrosis
Exposure of deep structures such as tendon within the wound base
reference.prognosis: Martorell ulcers are typically slow to heal and intensely painful, but with good blood pressure control, meticulous wound care and early skin grafting many will heal; recurrence and involvement of the contralateral leg are common.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the ulcer as pyoderma gangrenosum and treating with immunosuppression
Attributing the ulcer to large-vessel arterial disease despite normal pulses and ankle pressures
Providing inadequate analgesia for a characteristically severe pain
Taking a superficial biopsy that fails to sample the deep arteriolar pathology
Relying on strongly vasoconstricting antihypertensive agents that may impair skin perfusion
references: European Wound Management Association guidance on atypical wounds
